content: The provided text appears to be a list of references and citations related to the treatment of drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB), including studies, clinical trials, and guidelines. 1. The World Health Organization (WHO) has published comprehensive guidelines on the treatment of drug-resistant tuberculosis, including updates on the use of bedaquiline and delamanid in multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) management. These guidelines emphasize evidence-based approaches to improve treatment outcomes. 2. Bedaquiline has been shown to be effective in the treatment of MDR-TB, as highlighted in several studies. Its inclusion in treatment regimens has significantly improved patient outcomes, particularly in cases of rifampin-resistant TB. 3. Delamanid, another novel anti-TB drug, has demonstrated efficacy in treating MDR-TB. Clinical trials have shown its safety and effectiveness when used in combination with optimized background regimens. 4. Short-course, standardized treatment regimens for MDR-TB have been developed and tested in various settings, including Africa and Asia. These regimens are cost-effective, highly effective, and associated with high cure rates, as demonstrated in studies conducted in countries such as Cameroon, Niger, and South Africa. 5. The NExT Study, a multicenter randomized controlled trial, evaluated an all-oral 6-month regimen for MDR-TB. The results showed promising outcomes, with high cure rates and no relapses. 6. The combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid (BPaL regimen) has been studied extensively for the treatment of extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) and pre-XDR-TB. This regimen has shown high efficacy and safety in clinical trials. 7. Pharmacokinetic studies have explored the interactions between bedaquiline and antiretroviral drugs such as lopinavir/ritonavir and nevirapine in patients co-infected with HIV and TB. These studies provide guidance on dose adjustments to optimize treatment outcomes. 8. Linezolid has been found to be effective in treating XDR-TB, with studies in China demonstrating its safety, tolerability, and therapeutic efficacy. However, careful monitoring for adverse effects, such as lactic acidosis, is necessary. 9. The WHO has updated its definitions of treatment outcomes for TB, emphasizing the importance of standardized reporting to facilitate global comparisons and improve patient care. 10. Studies on the pharmacokinetics of anti-TB drugs, including bedaquiline and delamanid, in cerebrospinal fluid have provided insights into their use in treating TB meningitis. These findings are critical for managing life-threatening forms of TB. 11. The safety and efficacy of delamanid in children and adolescents with MDR-TB have been evaluated in clinical trials, leading to interim policy guidance from the WHO. 12. The cost-effectiveness of novel TB regimens, such as BPaL, has been assessed in various countries, including South Africa, Georgia, and the Philippines. These analyses highlight the potential for widespread implementation of these regimens in resource-limited settings. 13. The WHO has issued public calls for individual patient data to enhance the understanding of treatment outcomes for drug-resistant TB. This initiative aims to improve global TB management strategies. 14. Surveillance of adverse events associated with MDR-TB treatment has been conducted globally, providing valuable data on the safety profiles of anti-TB drugs. 15. Studies on the treatment of isoniazid-resistant TB have compared different regimens, including the use of isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide. These studies have informed clinical practice and optimized treatment strategies. 16. The hepatic safety of antibiotics used in TB treatment has been reviewed, with a focus on minimizing the risk of drug-induced liver injury in patients undergoing long-term therapy.
